title: You knit me together (Psalm 139)
hookLine: you know when I sit and rise; if I take the wings of morning, you are there

lines: A GRAINY PICTURE ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: On a lot of refrigerators there's a small, grainy, black-and-white picture held up by a magnet. You have to squint. A curve that might be a spine.

A blur that might be a hand. The people who put it there can tell you exactly which smudge is the nose. Before anyone has held this child, before anyone knows its laugh, it is already known, already loved.
Long before ultrasound, a psalm imagined that same hidden beginning, and claimed that someone was watching it closely.

teach.b: It begins, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off."
Sitting down, getting up, a thought before it's finished. Then the writer tries to imagine getting away. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?"
Up to heaven: you're there. Down to the grave: you're there.
"If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me."
The wings of the morning: fly as fast as the dawn moves across the sky, all the way to the far edge of the sea. Still held. Then the psalm goes inward, to the womb.
The King James says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb." The Hebrew verb can mean cover, or weave together, which is why many later translations say knit.

Two verses on, the writer says he was "curiously wrought" in secret, a phrase for embroidery, colored thread worked by hand. And in between, the line: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."
Fearfully here means with awe, the way you'd handle something precious. Then a surprise. Near the end, the psalm turns angry: the writer wants God to slay the wicked.
And right after, he stops and turns the searchlight on himself: "Search me, O God, and know my heart."

teach.h: I AM FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.
teach.b: See if there's any wicked way in me. A psalm that starts with being searched ends by asking for it.

how: Many Christians pray Psalm 139 as a prayer of being known by God; its last verses, "Search me, O God," are often prayed before confession or at the end of the day.

o: shaped out of clay by a potter's own hands
embroidered, worked by hand with colored thread
made strangely, in a way that puzzles people

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the King James Bible says knit in verse 13
it says covered. the Hebrew can mean cover or weave, so many later versions chose knit.
fearfully in verse 14 means with awe
made with the kind of care you'd give something precious.
the psalm stays gentle from start to finish
near the end it turns angry, then asks God to search the writer's own heart.

games.q: you've just asked God to slay the wicked. what does the psalm writer do next?
o: make a list of his enemies.
ask God to search his own heart.
games.why: "search me, O God, and know my heart." the psalm that began with being searched ends by asking for it.

practice: Place your hand flat on your heart, so you can feel it beating; it started before you knew you existed, and somebody, the psalm says, was paying attention even then. Feel the breath lift your hand a little, and let it down.
If you pray, say the line slowly, I am fearfully and wonderfully made; if you don't, simply feel how carefully you are put together, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Curiously wrought. The King James phrase for being embroidered, worked with colored thread, in secret, in the womb.

orig.note: Hebrew: I was embroidered, worked with colored thread. the King James Bible says "curiously wrought".

carryVoice: Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Handled with awe, like something precious. That's four hundred thirty-eight.
